Oversight is necessary to expose and prevent continued corruption, but Democrats cannot spend the next two years consumed by investigations, subpoenas and impeachment. Their priority must be improving Americans’ lives and getting the country back on track. Trump will soon be gone, and a third term remains his fantasy.

The same applies to Republicans. This is their opportunity to reclaim the party Trump took from them and replace those who enabled his worst abuses out of fear.

Democrats have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become the dominant political party nationally, as they have in California, by connecting the dots between Reagan’s plutocracy and Trump’s kleptocracy.

Reagan’s GOP championed tax cuts for the wealthy, corporate welfare and a judiciary increasingly protective of concentrated economic power. Trump has taken this philosophy further, turning political power into a vehicle for personal enrichment. Project 2025 embodies this evolution by dismantling safeguards against corporate influence and weakening institutions meant to protect the public.

The GOP’s electoral setbacks over economic discontent and corruption offer Democrats an opportunity to explain how the two are interconnected. For decades, Republican economic policies have enriched the wealthy at the expense of ordinary Americans. Citizens United amplified the political power of oligarchs, while the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling weakened presidential accountability.

If Democrats cannot capitalize on the backlash against this administration’s arrogance and conflicts of interest, they hardly deserve voters’ confidence. They must expose the connection between economic inequality, political corruption and concentrated wealth.

Americans are David confronting the GOP’s Goliath. Undoing the plutocracy Reagan helped build may take generations, but the struggle must begin now. The very soul of American democracy is at stake.

Our system of government was not formed to protect "democracy."  It was not formed to provide "services."  It was formed to protect individual rights from majoritarian predation.

What people seem to forget is that republicans don’t ever promise to deliver anything except for targeting the victim of the month. Their usual scapegoating of immigrants, trans kids, people of color, and whatever foreign countries we have a beef with, keeps their segment of the electorate engaged. As we recently saw with the SAVE act, the filibuster is the only thing that keeps the power of legislative majorities to inflict damage in check. 

On the flip side, the filibuster also makes it harder for Democrats to deliver on promises to make significant lasting changes that would benefit Americans. 

The calculation here is whether damage prevention outweighs the benefits, and if, given the vagaries of a fickle electorate, the risk is worth taking. Once we retire the filibuster it will not come back, as no one gives up power, willingly, or easily. 

For now, as much as I hate to admit it, I believe the filibuster needs to stay, as I don’t trust the American electorate to not shoot themselves in the foot given the chance.

When bills can't get through Congress, the party with popular ideas is disproportionately hurt. Democrats say they want to improve healthcare, raise the minimum wage, pay for childcare, lower college tuition, etc. etc.—all popular ideas. Voters don't believe them, though, because when they're in power, they can't deliver. 

Republicans, on the other hand, want to cut Medicare and Medicaid, privatize Social Security, give tax breaks to billionaires, etc. etc. All extremely unpopular ideas. But guess what? Voters don't believe them either, because the filibuster saves Republicans from their worse impulses.

Many people who voted for Trump in 2024 did so thinking he'd be constrained by Congress and establishment Republicans in his administration. Instead, he trampled over every norm and law that has constricted previous presidents and did all the unpopular things he promised. As bad as it was (and continues to be), voters clearly saw the consequences of their vote—and they acted accordingly in the last election. 

Getting rid of the filibuster certainly increases the risk that, like an unconstrained Trump, Republicans in Congress will be able to more easily accomplish their most diabolical objectives. But in the long run, democracy is healthier when people are able to connect their votes to tangible outcomes—good and bad.

A good PT taught me a stretching routine that I do every day without fail--and my low back pain is now minimal. Unfortunately, I also have spondylolisthesis, which occurs when one vertebra slips down over another. That is far more painful, but easy to combat with heat and movement. Leaning forward or standing too long exacerbates pain there. But moving around several times an hour rather than remaining in my chair, generally is all it takes to relieve the pain, along with a good heating pad. I wish someone had taught me all this when I was younger, but grateful for knowing now.

But for some reason I've never understood my mother was dead set against my sister having a peacoat and she really dug in her heels about it.  So my sister received a beautiful coat that was not a peacoat.  It looked like something Tricia Nixon would wear.   Definitely not what my sister wanted.  Tears and sobbing ensued.  I mean you would have thought that girl's entire world had just come tumbling down.  She wanted nothing to do with that coat.  I don't think she ever wore it.  In fact, she gave it away although my mother made her get it back.  So that's my peacoat story.  I don't know what our mother's problem was or whether my sister ever managed to get the coat she wanted, but I'll never forget how truly heartbroken she was that Christmas over not getting a peacoat.

comments.name: Metaphor

It is common in travel articles to read comments from readers about the spoiled rich people who fly First or Business Class. Fares paid for First and Business Class tickets are what keep fares for Economy affordable to everyone else. Delta and United have figured out that First and Business Class customers want to be able to sleep on long-haul flights. They pay a premium for lie-flat seats which then subsidize otherwise money-losing Economy tickets. Many other airlines in other countries do the same thing.

Conversely, all-Economy budget airlines in Asia, Europe, and other parts of the world offer cheap, cheap, cheap fares to everyone in return for bare-bones hard and soft product on relatively short flights.

You can't be both. Either you rely on premium class passengers to subsidize passengers in Economy, or you charge low fares for small seats and bare-bones service for everyone. Airlines that try to do both end up confusing the customer.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
This essay mentioned the need for remote access to critical systems.  Remote access is a big vulnerability.

Long ago computers were isolated boxes.  There was no remote access whatsoever, one had to physically come to the computer center to gain access.  So there was much more security.

It wouldn't kill us to cut back on remote access.  Also, to allow it only through secured hardwired private lines, not internet or dial up lines that anyone could access.  

Indeed, the open access of the internet, deliberately designed that way to encourage flexibility, is big vulnerability.  When my employer first allowed remote access, it was only through restricted secured private lines.  Access points had a hardwired terminal identification code.  But modern internet access doesn't support that.

This essay mentions "archaic" programming languages.  Well, why are they archaic?  It's only because the tech industry decreed it so.  That was a mistake.  We still use spoken and written English, even though some have suggested replacing it (say Esperanto).  

Lastly, exactly who are today's malevolent hackers?  Domestic ones should be prosecuted more so than now.  Foreign ones should be treated as an act of war or sabotage, as if a foreign agent snuck in with a bomb.

comments.name: joestat91
comments.body:
At some point in the interview, Ezra says "new A.I. systems keep coming out ...", as if AI systems "come out" like hurricanes or floods, beyond human control. Of course, they are not beyond human control (yet); they "come out" because Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg, Dario Amodei, and the others "put them out".

And, near the end of the interview, the interviewee says "cybersecurity is also an education and culture problem. And how do you fix people...". In other words, AI has been foisted on society by [the same guys as above] and now we have to "fix people".

Imagine if a new drug were foisted on society in this way, just rolling out like a flood and people having to be "fixed" to deal with it. Oxycodone anyone?

One last point: toward the end of the interview, the interviewee refers to  "solutions around things" and  "how nuanced these solutions are", referring to solutions of the problems laid out in the interview. First of all, I don't know what a "solution around" something is. You have a problem, and, if you solve it, you have a solution of the problem, not around the problem. And, secondly, if you have a problem, you don't have a solution until you have solved the problem. The problems discussed in this article have not been solved. So far there are no solutions of (not around) them.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
Good essay.

Yes, the choice to "bake software into every nook and cranny" was a bad one.  Contrary to myth and hype, we reached the point of diminishing returns and the cost of buying and installing hardware, software, and communications has now exceeded the benefits.

And yes, the focus on "move fast and break things", to rush design and roll out products without adequate design and testing was bad policy.  The computer designs were so sloppy, excessively complex, and excessive interconnected that trying to fix them only broke something else.  That is not surprising.

IBM learned it 60 years ago when it built a new operating system that didn't work because it was too complex; they had to redo it and scale it down.  But IBM fixed it before it was released to customers even though it made deliveries late.

So now the "digital deficit" has become due.  And it's a big debt because of the above two factors--being so dependent on computers and their sloppy design.

We can start by taking a pause and assess where we are.

Then we must demand better kill switches and air gaps so that problems don't cascade and better modularity and testing before products are released.  We need backup systems--maybe even pencil and paper, a pocket calculator, and landline phones--in case a key system fails. We should cease implementing new systems, especially A.I., until we get the mess under control. The business world will have to make do with less invasive advertising and invasions of privacy.

This resulted in a denial of service attack as every page had an error everytime it was called, on 17 servers worldwide times thousands of hits per hours. It was very easy to fix, but caused a fallback to an alternate simple home page for hours (until someone else came into the office after hours and found the cause,  to push out the image file to all the servers and restart them in normal mode). We had a pre-live site that could have been checked before the code push that would have shown the error, but apparently it was bypassed. Besides the no-Friday-push rule, we also instituted a no-day-before-holiday-push rule.

comments.body: The gap that hasn't been shrinking is the mortality gap between men and women, which has been growing for the last 2 decades. The gap is most profound for Black men, or even worst for Native American men. But by far the biggest factor is maleness, not race. Why is this not reported on? Because we have built institutions, multiple national institutions, dedicated to improving the health and well being of women and girls, and as of yet none, zero, for men, even though their outcomes are persistently worse. There is an assumption, propagated by the institutions built around women's health, that male health was the default setting of the health care industry. This is a self serving narrative meant to keep national dollars flowing to these institutions, while negating attention to men's health. It is no accident that the mortality gap is widening for men, and it will continue to do so until the narrative women's health neglect is maintained at the expense of any attention to men's health. We can and should pay attention to women's health problems, and wouldn't spend any less on women. But, we don't need to do so by maintaining the narrative that men's health has a long history of being front and center and that the neglect of women is unique. In almost every health parameter, men are doing worse. Why do we need the false narrative that disparities only happen to racial minorities and women. Men deserve attention, because they are dying, now, far younger and in greater numbers.

Everyone ranting that TIF is a “slush fund” has no clue. TIF funds either need to be spent within the geographic bounds of the district or they can be “ported” once to an adjacent district. But they can’t be transferred beyond that, so the funds from a district on the West Side can’t go to a downtown project - despite what you’re all screaming about. 

That said, TIF is a flawed tool because of the geographic limitations and rules about what it can fund. That’s why the City is trying to move to other funding sources, like bond, though the author chooses to overlook that policy shift. It’s easy for a Times writer who doesn’t know Chicago to cherry pick a bunch of bleak data and conditions from poverty-stricken neighborhoods that have resulted from decades of failed federal policies, racist real estate and finance practices and civil unrest, then blame the City for not turning that around in a few years. Meanwhile, there are no positive narratives related to the billions of dollars of incentives awarded to projects that result in new housing, retail, healthcare, local jobs and improvements to parks, schools and libraries - because yeah, Chicago is corrupt and always will be, right? 

Way to recycle a bunch of stale storylines that haven’t been relevant for years. And by the way, Ben Joravsky of the Chicago Reader basically made a career in journalism blasting the TIF program. There’s nothing you’ve said here that he hasn’t already written, except he understood it better.

Just wanted to inject a bit of more sober assessment of this development from Claude:
Caveats that matter for chips
*Seed layer: Measured resistance includes Nb seed, and NbP-only values come from subtracting control measurement. Raw effective resistivity of NbP plus seed is flat with width, not falling. "Better as it shrinks" result depends on that subtraction.
*Thick wires: Authors state that thicker NbP/Nb films do not beat conventional metals like copper. Advantage exists only for ultrathin ribbons with high surface-to-volume ratio.
Width uncertainty: Widths come from SEM and are probably overestimated. True conducting width is about 7 nm less than SEM value, due to Pd/Au coating and sidewall oxidation. That makes true width, and thus resistivity, uncertain.
*Substrate and seed dependence: Everything was grown on sapphire with a crystalline Nb seed. When NbP sat on more disordered Nb trilayer, its resistivity doubled. That is direct evidence of sensitivity to underlying layers. This is long way from a real chip.
*Roughness: Ribbons were not smooth, with about 2 nm line edge roughness and oxidised sidewalls. Authors present weak sensitivity to that disorder as a feature, but edge-state explanation rests largely on DFT modelling.
*Not yet shown: Paper covers single ribbons on test chips. It has no vias, multilayer wiring, dielectric integration, reliability testing or temperature-dependent aging. It also doesn't state the maximum ribbon length measured beyond about 5 µm.

Fifty years ago my employer used a computer with 128K in memory to run an entire hospital, to do all of its accounting and other services.  If the technology of the time could successfully run an entire hospital, why do we need all the bells and whistles of today?  Why is that today it takes a nurse literally 15 minutes to give a Tylenol, despite having a scanner to check both the bottle and wristband?  

That old hospital computer wasn't connected to anything.  Today's hospitals are interconnected, and its a great way for malware and ransomware to invade their computer and disrupt vital care.

Today's tech world is more pervasive than ever.  Yet no regulation whatsoever.  We inspect restaurant kitchens for sanitation, it's time for competent unbiased outsiders to audit computers.

Bottled water was introduced to the US as a mass market concept in the 1980's (exclusive of  what came from Europe like Evian or Perrier). A friend and I wondered about the staying power of such a concept. Holy cow, were we blind to the potential market.
Personally, I mostly choose room temperature filtered tap water, but I do like a cold carbonated water or club soda in lieu of a beer on occasion. 40 years later, mass marketed water has been a target of critics of plastic waste, but these elite waters, like wine, appear to be glass centric (although Evian and Perrier have been available in plastic for years).
I've always been curious so if the opportunity arises, I'd like to do a water tasting just to taste what the fuss is about. In the meantime, I'll enjoy my filtered tap water with moderate amounts of beer and wine, of course.

We had at least 2 dozen dorm- residing students over for a Thanksgiving spread and it was memorable. I do recall that finding a turkey was next to impossible but I think we found one eventually. The best fun was giggling over the late  Art Buchwald's classic article reprinted every year by the International Herald Tribune that tried to explain the story of Thanksgiving to French-speakers. It is a hoot.

comments.name: E Baptista
comments.body: While I appreciate that the plight of the Expat Thanksgiving has finally been acknowledged, this article is all about turkey. It misses the essence of the expat kitchen that runs substantially on substitutions: sweet potatoes and squash replace Libby's pumpkin in the pie. It fails to acknowledge the missing pieces: cranberries are tough to find beyond northern Europe. Also, as expat parents with children who have never been fed the lore of grade school finger-painted turkeys, we get to control the complex narrative of its origins. Translating the holiday isn't always easy. And stuffing? My kids aren't convinced.

comments.name: Claire Cain Miller
comments.body: I've been wondering if gender norms about who provides elder care would change with the younger generations, the same way norms around fatherhood have changed. Then, after covering the "S.N.L." sketch about Sister, I heard from a few different researchers that men in their teens and 20s were just as likely as young women to care for aging relatives. I’m curious whether this will continue as they age.

Cornucopia in the Age of AI

Prompting a frontier LLM can feel like tipping a cornucopia of drafts, hypotheses, and synthetic code onto a blank screen in seconds. Yet uncurated abundance easily becomes noise, making human judgment, explicit constraints, and verification essential so the model's overflowing output serves a deliberate goal rather than overwhelming decision-making.
